tool_groups.group: General AI assistants and research tools
tool_groups.overview: These six are horizontal assistants rather than departmental systems. Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT Enterprise compete as general chat-plus-agent platforms, while NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook) and Perplexity specialise in grounded research: the former over uploaded documents, the latter over the live web with citations. Overlap is growing: the big assistants offer deep research, file creation, connectors and agents; Perplexity offers third-party models (GPT, Gemini, Claude) inside its own interface. Enterprises usually standardise on the assistant bundled with their productivity suite, add one frontier chat platform for knowledge workers, and buy Perplexity Enterprise or Gemini Notebook as a niche research tool. Key procurement differences: training defaults (enterprise tiers exclude training by default; consumer tiers of Gemini, Claude and Perplexity differ), compliance coverage (varies by tier and sub-feature) and pricing model (flat seats versus seat-plus-usage). The claim that Gemini Enterprise routes work to Claude is not verified on an opened page.
tool_groups.verification_notes: Claude, Perplexity Enterprise and Google privacy/compliance claims were largely confirmed on opened vendor pages; Claude pricing and Enterprise Max pricing matched exactly. All openai.com and help.openai.com pages returned HTTP 403, so ChatGPT Enterprise data-handling, features and dates are unverified and its confidence is lowered to low; only third-party pricing (CloudZero) was confirmed. Several Google and Perplexity price points, dated news items and third-party-tracker figures could not be confirmed and are marked 'not verified' or removed. Trust-centre pages (Anthropic, Perplexity) and notebook.google returned no text, so FedRAMP/CSA/ISO-type claims resting on them were removed or flagged.

tool_groups.overview: All six tools are Microsoft products that share one identity, permission and compliance plane (Entra ID, Microsoft Graph, Purview), but they sit on two different licensing stacks. Microsoft 365 Copilot (now marketed as "Microsoft Copilot") is a per-user add-on, and Copilot in Word, Excel and Teams are not separate products but surfaces of that single licence; the free Copilot Chat tier gives enterprise-data-protected chat without the in-app features. Power BI Copilot and Power Automate belong to the Fabric/Power Platform stack, which is priced by capacity (Fabric CU) or by maker/bot licence plus consumption-based Copilot Credits, so the "Copilot" label hides very different cost models. Overlap is real: Teams recap competes with Teams Premium, Excel Copilot and Power BI Copilot both answer data questions, and Power Automate cloud flows compete with Copilot Studio agent flows. Enterprises already on Microsoft 365 E3/E5 usually standardise on the Copilot add-on (or the new E7 bundle) for knowledge workers, Power BI on Fabric capacity for analytics, and Power Automate Premium plus a governed Centre of Excellence for automation, while using Purview and DLP as the common control layer.
tool_groups.verification_notes: Core price points were confirmed on opened Microsoft pages (Power Automate Premium/Process/Hosted/Mining; Power BI Pro/PPU; AI Builder credit end date; COPILOT() retirement; Excel Python on 25 Aug 2026; EU Data Boundary exclusions for Anthropic and web queries; the product rename). The Microsoft 365 Copilot USD 30 price and Teams Premium USD 10 rest on independent sources because Microsoft's pricing page returned no figures, and E7 at USD 99 rests on Directions on Microsoft. Many dated 2026 feature claims, compliance certifications and government-cloud details could not be matched to an opened page and were removed or marked not verified, so confidence is capped at medium. Sources that were not opened or that failed (Techzine, Support how-to pages, vendor blogs, SOC 2/ISO pages) were dropped.

tool_groups.overview: These six tools form the output layer on top of general assistants and office suites: they turn text, data and documents into decks, graphics, prototypes and document summaries. Gamma and Canva compete for prompt-to-presentation and on-brand collateral (Gamma launched Gamma Imagine in March 2026 to take on Canva and Adobe, per TechCrunch). Adobe Firefly is the image/video engine marketed on commercial safety and Content Credentials. Acrobat AI Assistant is a different category (document comprehension over PDFs). Figma AI and FigJam AI are the product-design pair sharing one seat model and one AI-credit pool. Enterprises typically standardise on the suite they already license and allow one AI presentation tool under a Business/Enterprise tier where content training is contractually off. Recurring governance issues are consumption-based AI credits and default content training on lower tiers (verified for Figma and Gamma Pro; Canva and Adobe claims could not be re-opened and are marked not verified).
tool_groups.verification_notes: Gamma business and enterprise help-centre claims and Figma pricing, content-training defaults and certifications were confirmed on opened pages. Remaining cited news, release and review pages were only spot-checked for existence, not line by line.

tool_groups.overview: These six tools span IDE assistants (GitHub Copilot, Gemini Code Assist, Amazon Q Developer), an AI-native editor (Cursor), a terminal/cloud coding agent (Claude Code) and the open-source test framework (Playwright) that all of them now drive through MCP servers and agent definitions. They compete head-on in agentic multi-file coding, automated PR review and enterprise controls, and increasingly resell the same frontier models: Copilot and Cursor offer Claude, GPT and Gemini, while Claude Code itself runs inside VS Code and Cursor and on Bedrock, Google Cloud Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry. 2026 was a consolidation year: Google stopped selling new Code Assist subscriptions (Oct 9) in favour of Antigravity, AWS announced Q Developer's end of support for Kiro (Apr 30 2027), SpaceX folded Cursor into a Grok/X bundle (Oct 12), and GitHub moved to usage-metered AI Credits (June 1). Enterprises typically standardise on GitHub Copilot where GitHub is already the SCM, add Claude Code or Cursor for agentic work, keep the hyperscaler assistant matching their primary cloud, and adopt Playwright with its MCP server as the neutral QA layer. Procurement now has to track usage-based metering and model-provider retention terms as closely as seat prices.
tool_groups.verification_notes: Core pricing, tier and sunset claims for all six tools were re-checked against opened vendor pages and mostly held (Claude, Copilot credits, Cursor X Subscription tiers, Q/Kiro pricing, Gemini sunset dates). Weaker areas were fine-grained security attestations, changelog-level feature claims and secondary-source details, which could not be confirmed and were removed or marked not verified. Several cited pages could not be opened (github.com plans 403, Playwright v1.64.0 release 403, TechInformed) and were dropped from sources, as were cited pages not re-opened. Overall the group is reliable on prices and product status but should not be used for compliance certifications without checking each vendor's trust center.

dept_clusters.overview: All ten departments work mostly with long, unstructured, high-stakes documents (board papers, contracts, filings, case files, deal data rooms), so the shared AI pattern is summarise, compare, extract and draft, with a named human accountable for the output. The sources agree on the same controls: use approved enterprise tools, treat outputs as claims to verify (COSO's framing), keep an inventory of use cases, and scale human review to risk. Shared risks are privilege waiver and discoverability of AI transcripts, material non-public information and deal confidentiality, personal data in investigations (GDPR, whistleblower protections), and AI output that cannot be traced for audit or assurance. Evidence is thinnest for Office of the CEO, ERM and Ethics, where findings come from practitioner or vendor pieces rather than studies. Train together on a common module covering data classification, verification and prompt/output logging, with joint labs for Board Secretariat, Legal and Compliance (records and privilege), for Compliance, Internal Audit and ERM (controls evidence and COSO), and for Corporate Strategy and Corporate Development (scenario and deal analysis).
dept_clusters.verification_notes: I opened every cited URL (all returned OPENED) and checked the most surprising claims against the page text: EY adoption, Deloitte percentages, COSO six steps, Nestle and BCG figures, ACC survey, CSC survey, Ekimetrics figures, Optro 49%, Nasdaq Boardvantage, Harvey data-room claims. Nearly all checked claims held; corrections were small (wording, one unsupported use case, one unsupported sample size). Tool-capability claims (Datasite AI, CoCounsel, Acrobat AI, Now Assist) have no opened source and are flagged as not verified. Several sources are vendor or commentator pieces, so confidence is capped at medium for Compliance, Ethics and ESG.

dept_clusters.overview: Across the nine departments the dominant pattern is gen AI as a first-draft and synthesis layer (job descriptions, policy answers, feedback and incident summaries, workforce narratives) with a human owning the final decision. The evidence base is mostly vendor and practitioner material: Workday reports a Hackett Group figure that 66% of HR teams use gen AI, but measured outcomes are scarce, so trainees should treat time-saved claims as hypotheses to measure locally. Shared risks are special-category and employee personal data (GDPR), employment-discrimination law, and the EU AI Act and NYC Local Law 144 rules for hiring and worker-management AI, which apply even when a person gives final sign-off. Human reviewers are named as necessary in the payroll and facilities sources; the safety-specific human-review claims (Ibec) could not be verified. Recommended joint training: one common module on employee-data handling, bias testing and human-in-the-loop decisions for departments 11-17 and 19; a second shared lab on HR-knowledge-base prompting for 11, 14, 16 and 18 (employee FAQs, ticket routing); and a safety/facilities pairing for 18 and 19 on incident and work-order summarisation.

Corrections were small: Metaview's AI-disclosure duty falls on providers, Colorado enforcement is on hold, one MiHCM guidance claim was unsupported, and department 19 lost its Ibec claims because the page returned HTTP 403. dept_clusters.overview: All eight departments turn structured ledger, bank, spend or contract data into drafts, summaries and exception lists that a named human then reviews, so the shared skill is verification: reperforming numbers, tying output to source and documenting who signed off. Shared risks are confident-but-wrong output, material non-public information, personal and bank data, and weak evidence trails; sources describe COSO's February 2026 generative-AI control guidance and a Workiva finding that 1 in 4 executives said an AI error reached investors or the board. Microsoft itself warns against relying on Copilot in Excel for finance decisions. Training should be joint for a common core (data classification, review gates, prompt and evidence logging) and for three pairings: FP&A, Accounting and Treasury (variance, forecast and close narratives in spreadsheets); AP, Procurement and Vendor Management (P2P documents, contracts, supplier data and fraud signals); and FP&A with Investor Relations (earnings numbers and narrative consistency). Tax and IR need their own legal and disclosure modules.

dept_clusters.overview: All eight departments use AI for the same core jobs: research and synthesis, personalised first drafts, call and meeting summarisation, and reporting on CRM or campaign data. Sellers and marketers also report that data quality, not the model, is the limiting factor (Salesforce: 74% of AI-using sales teams prioritise data hygiene). Shared risks are personal data of prospects and contacts (UK/EU GDPR, PECR or e-privacy marketing consent), recorded-call consent (wiretap litigation against AI notetakers), confidential pipeline, pricing and customer data, and unverified AI claims reaching buyers. Vendor-reported gains are large but self-reported, and independent analyses of ad automation are more mixed, so training should teach measuring incremental results against a baseline. Train together on a common module covering CRM data hygiene, consent and recording rules, citation-checked research and a human review gate before external sending. Sales Ops with the two sales teams, Marketing with Digital Marketing, and Research with BD and Pre-Sales are natural pairings for hands-on labs.

One use case (Cyera registrations) and the SOX claim had no support and were removed or flagged; the ICO "absolute right to object to profiling" wording was corrected to what the page says. Several tool-fit claims (Einstein, NotebookLM, Canva, Power BI Copilot, RFP platforms) remain unverified and are labelled so. dept_clusters.overview: All five departments turn unstructured customer signals (tickets, calls, surveys, interview notes, feedback, usage data) into summaries, drafts and prioritised actions, and in each one the tool's output is a draft that a human must validate. The shared risks are customer personal data (GDPR/UK GDPR), unapproved "shadow AI" use, and confident but wrong output. Wrong output includes misread sentiment, invented user insight and mis-scored churn risk. Vendor-reported results (resolution rates, retention gains) are marketing claims and should not be used as training benchmarks. Customer Success, Support and CX should train together on voice-of-customer synthesis, data handling and human escalation rules. Product Management and Product Design & UX Research should train together on evidence-grounded PRDs, research synthesis and acceptance criteria. A joint cross-cluster session could use one shared feedback dataset, taking it from support tickets to themes to backlog items.

dept_clusters.overview: All six departments use AI in the same way. An assistant drafts code, tests, infrastructure templates, runbooks or knowledge articles. A human then verifies the draft against something that can pass or fail: a test run, a plan or dry-run, or telemetry. Claude Code's own best-practice guidance says to give the agent a check it can run. Shared risks are source code and credentials pasted into prompts, hallucinated or insecure output, and agents acting with broad permissions on production systems or ERP. Departments 41-44 should train together on agentic coding, verification gates and secrets hygiene, and 43-45 together on cloud and ticket-system tooling. Department 46 should join 45 for ticket and knowledge workflows, and 46 should train with Finance on SAP data. Evidence quality is uneven. Most quantified claims come from vendors or from a single company's self-report, so managers should measure their own baselines. ServiceNow, Salesforce, Dynatrace and Cursor claims could not be verified because those pages could not be opened.
dept_clusters.verification_notes: All cited URLs opened, and most specific claims matched their sources (Zoominfo figures, Accenture RCT design, Meta 73%, AWS, Google, Azure, Datadog, Security Copilot, SAP). Errors found were misattributions and extrapolations rather than fabrications. Remaining weaknesses are heavy reliance on vendor pages and a single source for department 46, so the low confidence there and in 42 and 45 stands. Cursor, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Dynatrace and GitHub Copilot for pipeline files were not checked against any opened page.

dept_clusters.overview: All five departments sit on sensitive data and on the platforms that hold it, so the strongest pattern is vendor-embedded AI that inherits existing access controls (Security Copilot, Purview, Snowflake RBAC, Power BI semantic models) and works best on well-prepared metadata. Shared risks are over-sharing through broad permissions, unverified AI output feeding decisions (alert verdicts, generated SQL, dashboard answers), and agents taking actions, so human approval gates and evaluation datasets are common requirements. Departments 47 and 48 should train together on SOC and governance handoffs and AI-agent oversight, and 49, 50 and 51 on semantic-layer preparation, answer validation and evaluation-driven development. All five should share one module on governing AI (NIST AI RMF and its generative AI profile) and on data classification. Research limit: most claims are vendor-reported, and regulatory hooks beyond NIST are general knowledge, not verified.
dept_clusters.verification_notes: All eleven distinct sources opened successfully. Core vendor claims (550%, 200 hours, ISO 42001, 98%/70% figures, CORTEX_USER granted to PUBLIC, Cortex no-training, NIST AI 600-1, Power BI geographic and SKU restrictions, Foundry governance, Purview AI app coverage) were confirmed on the cited pages. Several details were overstated or unsupported and were softened or removed, most notably the Genie Code rename, KQL, one-click policies and the Purview investigation scenario. Figures remain vendor-reported, and regulatory hooks other than NIST remain unverified, so confidence stays medium.

Statements marked "not verified" come from general practice, not from an opened page. The expected shared pattern is that all seven departments turn semi-structured operational records (tickets, status updates, SOPs, audit findings, incident logs) into summaries, drafts and exception lists. The shared risks are confidential project, supplier and incident data, personal data in tickets and change feedback (GDPR), and unreviewed AI output entering formal records (SLAs, quality records, recovery plans). Suggested joint training is a shared module on process and ticket data hygiene and human review of AI outputs. Joint sessions are also suggested for 55/56/58 (process and SOP work), 54/57 (portfolio and change reporting), and 59 with 55 (incident communications). All of this needs verification before it goes into the handbook. A follow-up with fresh search budget is recommended.
